title: The first wars: from Morgarten to the Stoss
card: How small valleys and towns beat Habsburg armies and nobles between 1315 and 1405.

stops.title: Morgarten: ambush at the lake
text: Schwyz quarrelled with Habsburg for years. One cause was a long fight over pasture land with the abbey of Einsiedeln, which Habsburg protected.
In November 1315 Duke Leopold I of Habsburg led an army towards Schwyz. Near the upper end of Lake Ägeri, men from Schwyz attacked the army on a narrow path and beat it.
Three weeks later, Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden renewed their alliance at Brunnen. For centuries people saw this pact of 1315 as the start of the Confederation.

places.name: Morgarten (Schornen)
places.note: Schwyz beats Duke Leopold I of Habsburg

sources.title: HLS: Morgartenkrieg

sources.supports: Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden made a new alliance at Brunnen on 9 December 1315 (place Brunnen)

sources.title: HLS: Morgartenkrieg

uncertain: The attack took place on a narrow path.

stops.title: Laupen: Bern against the nobles
text: Bern grew fast and took land and people from the nobles. The nobles, the town of Fribourg and the bishops of Basel and Lausanne joined forces against Bern. Bern held the small town of Laupen, and from 10 June 1339 their army laid siege to it.
On 21 June 1339 Bern, helped by troops from Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden and Solothurn, beat the nobles' army near Laupen.
The peace of 1340 made Bern the strongest power in the region. In 1353 Bern made a lasting alliance with the forest valleys.

places.name: Laupen (Bramberg)

sources.title: HLS: Laupenkrieg

sources.title: HLS: Laupenkrieg

sources.title: HLS: Laupenkrieg

sources.supports: Bern held Laupen, which was besieged from 10 June 1339 (place Laupen town)

sources.supports: On 21 June 1339 Bern was helped by troops from Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden and Solothurn (layer Bern and its helpers)

sources.supports: In 1353 Bern made a lasting alliance with the forest valleys

uncertain: The battle took place on the Bramberg hill near Neuenegg (HLS names the place 'Wyden').

stops.title: Sempach: the duke is killed
text: By 1353 eight places were allied: Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, Lucerne, Zurich, Zug, Glarus and Bern. Lucerne took Habsburg towns and land around it.
Duke Leopold III of Habsburg marched against Lucerne. On 9 July 1386 the Confederates beat his army near Sempach. The duke died in the battle, with many nobles.
Habsburg lost its strength south of the Rhine. Step by step, it lost its land in this area to the Confederates.

layers.name: Eight places
layers.label: The eight allied places (today's cantons, rough)

places.name: Sempach
places.note: Confederates win; Duke Leopold III killed

sources.title: HLS: Eidgenossenschaft

sources.supports: Lucerne took Habsburg towns and land around it

sources.supports: On 9 July 1386 the Confederates met his army near Sempach (place Sempach)

sources.title: HLS: Sempacherkrieg
sources.quote: Mit Herzog Leopold III. fiel eine grosse Zahl regionaler Adliger
sources.supports: The duke died in the battle, with many nobles

sources.title: HLS: Sempacherkrieg
sources.quote: schwächte Habsburg-Österreich so sehr, dass es seine Herrschaftspositionen in den Gebieten südlich des Hochrheins langfristig nicht halten konnte
sources.supports: Habsburg lost its strength and, step by step, its land south of the Rhine

stops.title: Näfels: Glarus frees itself
text: The war went on. In February 1388 Habsburg troops took the small town of Weesen by surprise.

On 9 April 1388 a Habsburg army broke into the valley of Glarus. About 400 men from Glarus, with a few dozen from Schwyz and Uri, attacked the army while it plundered. The army fled, and the bridge at Weesen broke under the fleeing men.
Glarus was now free of Habsburg rule. People in Glarus still walk to the battle site each year (the 'Näfelser Fahrt').

sources.title: HLS: Näfels, Schlacht bei
sources.quote: den österreichischen Überfall ( Mordnacht vom 21./22. Februar 1388) auf das von den Glarnern und Eidgenossen ab 1386 besetzte Städtchen Weesen
sources.supports: In February 1388 Habsburg troops took Weesen by surprise

sources.title: HLS: Näfels, Schlacht bei
sources.quote: Die etwa 400 Glarner, verstärkt durch einige Dutzend Schwyzer und Urner
sources.supports: About 400 men from Glarus with a few dozen from Schwyz and Uri

sources.title: HLS: Näfels, Schlacht bei
sources.quote: griffen von hier aus, begünstigt durch Nebel und Schneetreiben, das plündernde Ritterheer an
sources.supports: They attacked the army while it plundered

sources.title: HLS: Näfels, Schlacht bei
sources.quote: die beim Zusammenbruch der Brücke bei Weesen in grosser Zahl in der Maag ertranken
sources.supports: The army fled and the bridge at Weesen broke

sources.title: HLS: Sempacherkrieg
sources.quote: Glarus befreite sich dank des Siegs in der Schlacht bei Näfels am 9. April 1388 von der österreichischen Herrschaft.
sources.supports: Glarus was now free of Habsburg rule (layer Glarus)

sources.title: HLS: Näfels, Schlacht bei

sources.supports: People in Glarus still walk to the battle site each year (Näfelser Fahrt)

sources.quote: Der Sieg der Eidgenossen in der Schlacht bei Sempach am 9. Juli 1386
sources.supports: Place Sempach: the Confederates won in 1386

stops.title: The Sempach Letter
text: In 1393 the eight places and Solothurn agreed on common rules for war, the 'Sempacherbrief' (Sempach Letter). For example, soldiers must not attack churches, monasteries and women, they may plunder only after a victory, and deserters are judged.
The letter also forbade all violence among the Confederates. It was one of the first agreements that all eight places signed together.

layers.name: Eight places
layers.label: The eight places of the Sempach Letter (rough)

sources.title: HLS: Sempacherbrief
sources.quote: Abkommen zwischen Zürich, Luzern, Bern, Solothurn, Zug, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden und Glarus vom 10.7.1393.
sources.supports: In 1393 the eight places and Solothurn made the Sempach Letter (layer Eight places)

sources.title: HLS: Sempacherbrief
sources.quote: Geplündert werden durfte erst nach erfochtenem Sieg, dabei sollten Kirchen, Klöster und Frauen geschont werden
sources.supports: Rules for war: plunder only after victory; spare churches, monasteries and women

sources.title: HLS: Sempacherbrief

sources.supports: Deserters are judged

sources.supports: Place Näfels: battle of 1388

stops.title: Vögelinsegg: Appenzell rises
text: The farmers of Appenzell had to pay taxes to the abbot of St. Gallen. They refused and made an alliance with Schwyz.

On 15 May 1403, near Speicher, the men of Appenzell, led by captains from Schwyz, beat the army of the abbot and the towns around Lake Constance. After this, the town of St. Gallen took the side of Appenzell.

layers.label: Land of the abbot of St. Gallen (rough)

places.name: Vögelinsegg
places.note: Appenzell beats the abbot of St. Gallen

sources.supports: The farmers of Appenzell had to pay dues to the abbot of St. Gallen (layer Abbey of St. Gallen)

sources.title: HLS: Appenzeller Kriege (1401-1429)
sources.quote: setzte Appenzell – anders als die Stadt St. Gallen – seinen Widerstand fort und trat 1403 in ein Landrecht mit Schwyz
sources.supports: Appenzell refused and made an alliance with Schwyz (layer Appenzell, ally of Schwyz)

sources.supports: Appenzell, led by captains from Schwyz, beat the abbot and the towns around Lake Constance

sources.supports: After this, the town of St. Gallen took the side of Appenzell

stops.title: Stoss: Habsburg is beaten again
text: Then Austria (Habsburg) joined the war. On 17 June 1405 an Austrian army of about 1,200 men climbed towards Appenzell over the Stoss pass above Altstätten.
About 400 men of Appenzell waited above the path. They threw stones and attacked with halberds, and the army fled. The story of the hero Uli Rotach comes from later legend.

After the victory Appenzell and the town of St. Gallen founded the 'League above the Lake' (Bund ob dem See). It broke up in 1408. In 1411 Appenzell made an alliance with the Confederates (without Bern).

sources.title: HLS: Stoss, Schlacht am

sources.supports: Uli Rotach is a legend linked to the battle

sources.title: HLS: Appenzeller Kriege (1401-1429)

notes: Areas are today's cantons and districts; the real territories of 1315-1405 were smaller and patchy. Habsburg land is shown only roughly. The exact place of the Morgarten battle is debated; the point is at the memorial at Schornen. Laupen point: Bramberg memorial near Neuenegg. The Sempach Letter step (1393) is context, not a battle.

title: The 15th century: civil war, Burgundy and the Empire
card: From the Old Zurich War to Charles the Bold and the Swabian War: the century that made the Swiss feared soldiers.

stops.title: Old Zurich War: St. Jakob an der Sihl
text: In 1436 the last Count of Toggenburg died without heirs. Zurich and Schwyz both wanted his land. The quarrel became a war between the Confederates.

In 1442 Zurich made an alliance with the Habsburg king Frederick III. On 22 July 1443 the Confederates beat the Zurich troops at St. Jakob an der Sihl, just outside the town. The mayor of Zurich, Rudolf Stüssi, was killed.

sources.title: HLS: Zurich, guerre de
sources.quote: La succession du comte Frédéric VII de Toggenbourg, mort sans héritier en 1436, fut la cause directe de la guerre.
sources.supports: In 1436 the last Count of Toggenburg died without heirs; this caused the war

sources.title: HLS: Zurich, guerre de
sources.quote: Zurich et Schwytz dont il était combourgeois, les Habsbourg, dont il détenait des gages
sources.supports: Zurich and Schwyz both claimed his land

sources.title: HLS: Zurich, guerre de
sources.quote: Les autres Confédérés (les Uranais et les Unterwaldiens à la dernière minute seulement) s'étaient rangés au côté de Schwytz.
sources.supports: The quarrel became a war between Zurich and the other Confederates (layer Confederates)

sources.title: HLS: Zurich, guerre de
sources.quote: à conclure une alliance avec lui le 17 juin 1442
sources.supports: In 1442 Zurich made an alliance with Frederick III of Habsburg (layer Zurich, allied with Habsburg)

sources.title: HLS: St. Jakob an der Sihl, Schlacht bei
sources.quote: Am 22. Juli kam es zur Schlacht.
sources.supports: The battle took place on 22 July 1443 (place St. Jakob an der Sihl)

sources.title: HLS: St. Jakob an der Sihl, Schlacht bei
sources.quote: Die Zürcher zogen sich in die Stadt zurück. Sie verloren 300 Mann, unter ihnen Bürgermeister Rudolf Stüssi.
sources.supports: The Confederates beat the Zurich troops outside the town; mayor Rudolf Stüssi was killed

stops.title: St. Jakob an der Birs
text: The Habsburg king Frederick III called in the 'Armagnacs', a large army of French mercenaries led by the Dauphin Louis (later King Louis XI).

On 26 August 1444 a Confederate force of about 1,500 men attacked them near Basel. After a long fight almost all the Confederates were killed. HLS gives about 1,200 Confederate dead and about 2,000 Armagnac dead.
But the French army did not march on. On 28 October 1444 the Dauphin made peace at Ensisheim. In 1450 the war ended, and Zurich had to leave its alliance with Habsburg.

sources.title: HLS: St. Jakob an der Birs, Schlacht bei
sources.quote: Von Kg. Friedrich III. herbeigerufen, aber ohne förml. Bündnisvertrag, rückte im Sommer 1444 das franz. Söldnerheer der im Hundertjährigen Krieg auftragslos gewordenen Armagnaken
sources.supports: King Frederick III called in the Armagnacs, a French mercenary army (layer France and Armagnacs)

sources.title: HLS: St. Jakob an der Birs, Schlacht bei
sources.quote: unter der Führung des Dauphins (später Kg. Ludwig XI.) ins Elsass ein und legte sich vor Basel
sources.supports: The army was led by the Dauphin Louis and came near Basel

sources.title: HLS: St. Jakob an der Birs, Schlacht bei
sources.quote: Eine eidg. Schar von ca. 1'500 Mann, die gerade die Farnsburg belagerte, zog ihnen in der Frühe des 26. August ohne Auftrag entgegen.
sources.supports: On 26 August 1444 about 1,500 Confederates attacked them (place St. Jakob an der Birs)

sources.title: HLS: St. Jakob an der Birs, Schlacht bei
sources.quote: Auf der Seite der Armagnaken fielen ca. 2'000, auf eidg. Seite 1'200 Mann.
sources.supports: About 1,200 Confederate dead and about 2,000 Armagnac dead

sources.title: HLS: St. Jakob an der Birs, Schlacht bei
sources.quote: Der Dauphin schloss in Ensisheim am 28.10.1444 mit Basel und den Eidgenossen Frieden.
sources.supports: Peace at Ensisheim on 28 October 1444

sources.title: HLS: Zurich, guerre de
sources.quote: un accord de paix définitif en 1450. Zurich rentra en possession de son territoire à l'exception des Höfe, mais dut rompre son alliance avec l'Autriche
sources.supports: In 1450 the war ended and Zurich had to leave the alliance with Habsburg (layer Zurich)

sources.title: HLS: St. Jakob an der Sihl, Schlacht bei
sources.quote: Die Zürcher zogen sich in die Stadt zurück.
sources.supports: Place St. Jakob an der Sihl: Confederates won in 1443

stops.title: Charles the Bold of Burgundy
text: Duke Charles the Bold of Burgundy ruled lands in Burgundy and in the Netherlands. He wanted to join these two parts into one state. In 1469 Habsburg gave him its land in Alsace as a pledge.

Now Burgundy was a direct neighbour of the Confederates. Bern feared that Charles could close its trade roads, and King Louis XI of France was his enemy. In 1474 the Confederates and Austria made peace, and the Confederates declared war on Burgundy. On 13 November 1474 they and their allies won at Héricourt, west of Basel.

sources.title: HLS: Burgund (Herzogtum)
sources.quote: Seine beiden Schwerpunkte waren das feudal geprägte Alt-Burgund und die eher städtisch-bürgerlich bestimmten Niederlande
sources.supports: Burgundy had two parts: Burgundy and the Netherlands (layer Duchy of Burgundy)

sources.title: HLS: Burgund (Herzogtum)

sources.supports: Charles wanted to join his two groups of lands

sources.title: HLS: Burgunderkriege
sources.quote: erhielt als Gegenleistung die vorderösterreichischen Besitzungen ( Vorderösterreich ) im Elsass als Pfand (Vertrag von Saint-Omer, 9. Mai 1469)
sources.supports: In 1469 Habsburg gave Charles land in Alsace as a pledge

sources.title: HLS: Burgunderkriege
sources.quote: Zugleich fürchtete Bern, dass der neue Nachbar Burgund die Handelsstrassen durch das schweizerische Mittelland zu den Genfer Messen sperren könnte.
sources.supports: Burgundy became a neighbour; Bern feared for its trade roads

sources.title: HLS: Burgunderkriege
sources.quote: Der mit Burgund verfeindete Ludwig XI.
sources.supports: King Louis XI of France was an enemy of Burgundy (layer France)

sources.title: HLS: Burgunderkriege
sources.quote: einen Vertragsentwurf, der die langjährigen Feindseligkeiten zwischen Habsburg und den Eidgenossen beendigen sollte
sources.supports: In 1474 the Confederates and Austria made peace

sources.title: HLS: Héricourt, Schlacht von
sources.quote: Die Eidgenossen und ihre Verbündeten (Niedere Vereinigung, österr. Städte des Elsass, schwäb. Reichsstädte) brachen unmittelbar nach der Kriegserklärung an Karl den Kühnen
sources.supports: The Confederates and allies declared war on Charles (layer Confederates and allies)

sources.title: HLS: Burgunderkriege
sources.quote: seinen Abschluss am 13. November 1474 mit einem Sieg über die Burgunder in der Schlacht von Héricourt fand
sources.supports: Victory at Héricourt on 13 November 1474 (place Héricourt)

stops.title: Grandson: the duke flees
text: In February 1476 Charles took the town and castle of Grandson. He had the Bernese garrison hanged or drowned in the lake.
On 2 March 1476 the Confederate army met his army near Concise. The Burgundian troops panicked and ran away. The Confederates plundered his camp and took a rich booty.

sources.title: HLS: Grandson, Schlacht bei
sources.quote: nahm zuerst Yverdon, dann die Stadt G. (21.2.) und das Schloss (am 28.2.) ein
sources.supports: In February 1476 Charles took the town and castle of Grandson (place Grandson)

sources.title: HLS: Grandson, Schlacht bei
sources.quote: Die Berner Garnison liess er erhängen oder im See ertränken.
sources.supports: He had the Bernese garrison hanged or drowned

sources.title: HLS: Grandson, Schlacht bei
sources.quote: Am 2. März verlegte Karl rund 20'000 Mann von G. in die Nähe von Concise in ein ungünstiges Gelände.
sources.supports: On 2 March 1476 the armies met near Concise

sources.title: HLS: Grandson, Schlacht bei

sources.supports: The Burgundian troops panicked and ran away

sources.title: HLS: Grandson, Schlacht bei

stops.title: Nancy: the end of Charles
text: René II of Lorraine took back Nancy, and Charles laid siege to it from October 1476. René hired more than 8,000 Confederate soldiers.

On 5 January 1477 René's army beat Charles near Nancy. Charles was killed after the battle. His lands were split: the King of France took the Duchy of Burgundy, and Habsburg got the largest part of his other lands.
After these wars the princes of Europe wanted Swiss soldiers. Hiring out soldiers (mercenary service) became a big business for the Confederates.

text: Uri had held the Leventina valley south of the Gotthard pass since about 1440. In 1466 Milan gave it to Uri for good, but later the Duke of Milan refused to hand it over. In November 1478 Uri, and then the other Confederates, crossed the Gotthard.

On 28 December 1478 a small force of about 175 men and 400 men from the Leventina stayed behind at Giornico. With a trick, it beat a much larger army from Milan. People in Ticino call it the 'battle of the big stones'.
Milan gave up the Leventina, and Uri ruled it again. Bellinzona stayed with Milan for now.

Maximilian had to make peace. The Peace of Basel (22 September 1499) ended the war. The Confederates stayed in the Empire, but in practice the new imperial court no longer had power over them.
Basel and Schaffhausen joined the Confederation in 1501, and Appenzell in 1513.

title: The Italian Wars: Swiss soldiers in Lombardy
card: From 1500 to 1525 Swiss armies fought for Milan, beat France at Novara and lost at Marignano and Pavia.

stops.title: Milan, France and Swiss soldiers
text: Around 1500 the King of France and the Duke of Milan fought over Milan. Both sides hired Swiss soldiers.
In April 1500, at Novara, Swiss soldiers stood on both sides. The Swiss of Duke Ludovico Sforza refused to fight. The duke fell into French hands. France ruled Milan.
In the same year Uri, Schwyz and Nidwalden took Bellinzona. France accepted this in 1503.

stops.title: Novara: the high point
text: In 1513 King Louis XII of France sent an army to take Milan back. Swiss troops held Novara.
On 6 June 1513 the Swiss attacked the French army near Novara and beat it. HLS calls this the high point of Swiss military power.

In the same year a Swiss army marched into France and laid siege to Dijon. The town gave up, and France promised to give up Milan and to pay money. The Swiss army went home early, and the king then broke the treaty.

stops.title: Marignano: the turning point
text: In 1515 the new King of France, Francis I, came with a strong army with cavalry and many cannons. Some Swiss captains, from Bern, Solothurn and Fribourg, made a treaty with the king at Gallarate that promised money. Others did not accept it and fought.

On 13 and 14 September 1515 the armies met at Marignano (today Melegnano), south-east of Milan. On the second morning Venetian troops came to help the French, and the Swiss lost. HLS gives 9,000 to 10,000 Swiss dead.
France took Milan. The Swiss lost to the French guns and to the help from Venice.

stops.title: The Perpetual Peace
text: On 29 November 1516 the Confederates and France signed the 'Perpetual Peace' at Fribourg. The Swiss gave up their protection of Milan.
They kept Bellinzona, Lugano, Locarno, Mendrisio and the Maggia valley. These lands are today the canton of Ticino. Graubünden kept the Valtellina. The Ossola valley went back to Milan.
In 1521 the Confederates made an alliance with France. From now on France hired many Swiss soldiers.

sources.supports: In 1521 an alliance with France that provided Swiss soldiers

sources.title: HLS: Marignano, Schlacht von
sources.quote: Die Eidgenossen, die vorzugsweise im Schlachthaufen kämpften, wurden durch die Artillerie und die Ankunft der Venezianer besiegt.
sources.supports: Place Marignano: the French won

stops.title: Bicocca: guns beat pikes
text: Now the Swiss fought for France against Emperor Charles V. Both wanted Milan.

On 27 April 1522 the Swiss and the French fought the imperial army at Bicocca, north of Milan. The enemy waited behind a ditch and a wall and fired with handguns (arquebuses). France and the Swiss lost the battle.

places.note: Imperial army beats French and Swiss

sources.title: HLS: Bicocca, Schlacht bei
sources.quote: 1521 schlossen die eidg. Orte mit dem franz. Kg. Franz I. in Luzern eine Allianz
sources.supports: Now the Swiss fought for France (layer France)

sources.title: HLS: Bicocca, Schlacht bei
sources.quote: einem Ort nördlich Mailands, bei der sich die Heere des franz. Königs, der im Begriff stand, Mailand zurückzuerobern, und Ks. Karls V. gegenüberstanden
sources.supports: Bicocca is north of Milan; France fought Emperor Charles V over Milan (place Bicocca; layer Milan)

sources.title: HLS: Bicocca, Schlacht bei
sources.quote: Der Kampf gegen die kaiserl. Truppen unter der Leitung von Prospero Colonna fand am 27.4.1522 statt. Frankreich und die Eidgenossen verloren die Schlacht.
sources.supports: On 27 April 1522 France and the Swiss lost

sources.title: HLS: Ewiger Frieden
sources.quote: Auf diese Weise gelangte das Gebiet des späteren Kt. Tessin definitiv, Mendrisio ab 1521, an die Eidgenossenschaft.
sources.supports: Layer Swiss lands in the south

stops.title: Pavia: the end of expansion
text: King Francis I tried again. From October 1524 he laid siege to Pavia. About 8,000 Swiss served in his army.
On 24 February 1525 an imperial army attacked and won. The king himself was taken prisoner.

Bicocca and Pavia ended Swiss plans to rule in northern Italy. The Reformation now divided the Confederates. From here on they no longer made war to win land abroad, but many Swiss still served as mercenaries.

layers.name: Milan

sources.quote: Kg. Franz I. von Frankreich belagerte ab dem 28.10.1524 P. mit 29'000 Mann, darunter 8'000 Schweizern unter Hans von Diesbach.
sources.supports: From October 1524 Francis I laid siege to Pavia; about 8,000 Swiss in his army (place Pavia)

sources.title: HLS: Pavia, Schlacht bei

sources.supports: On 24 February 1525 an imperial army attacked

sources.title: HLS: Pavia, Schlacht bei

sources.supports: The imperial army won; the king was taken prisoner

sources.title: HLS: Bicocca, Schlacht bei
sources.quote: Diese Niederlage und diejenige von Pavia 1525 bedeuteten das Ende der eidg. Expansionspolitik in Norditalien.
sources.supports: Bicocca and Pavia ended Swiss plans in northern Italy (place Bicocca)

sources.title: HLS: Marignano, Schlacht von

sources.supports: Many Swiss still served as mercenaries (for France)

sources.title: HLS: Marignano, Schlacht von
sources.quote: Nach Marignano gaben die eidgenössischen Orte ihre Expansionspolitik auf.
sources.supports: They no longer made war to win land abroad (place Marignano)

sources.title: HLS: Novara, Schlachten bei

sources.supports: Place Novara: Swiss win

notes: Duchy of Milan drawn with today's Italian provinces (Milano, Monza, Lodi, Pavia, Como, Lecco, Varese, Novara, Cremona): rough. title: Civil wars: faith and farmers
card: After the Reformation the Confederates fought each other four times, and in 1653 the farmers rose against the towns.

stops.title: First Kappel War: the milk soup
text: The Reformation split the Confederates. Zurich, Bern, Basel and Schaffhausen became Protestant (Reformed). The five inner places, Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden and Zug, stayed Catholic.
In 1529 Schwyz burned a Reformed pastor, Jakob Kaiser. Zurich went to war. The armies met near Kappel, but they did not fight. A story says that soldiers of both sides ate milk soup together.
The First Peace of Kappel (26 June 1529) favoured the Reformed side.

places.name: Kappel am Albis
places.note: First Peace of Kappel, no battle

sources.title: HLS: Kappelerkriege
sources.quote: zwischen den reformierten Städten – insbesondere Zürich und Bern – und den altgläubigen fünf inneren Orten der Eidgenossenschaft (Luzern, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden und Zug)
sources.supports: The Reformation split the Confederates; the five inner places stayed Catholic (layers Reformed, Catholic)

sources.title: HLS: Kappelerkriege
sources.quote: Der Durchbruch der Reformation in Bern, Basel und Schaffhausen 1528-1529
sources.supports: Bern, Basel and Schaffhausen became Reformed

sources.title: HLS: Kappelerkriege
sources.quote: Zum Auslöser des Ersten Kappelerkriegs wurde die Verbrennung des reformierten Pfarrers Jakob Kaiser in Schwyz.
sources.supports: In 1529 Schwyz burned the Reformed pastor Jakob Kaiser

sources.title: HLS: Kappelerkriege
sources.quote: Zürich erklärte den fünf Orten am 8. Juni 1529 den Krieg und zog mit seiner Hauptmacht nach Kappel an der Zuger Grenze
sources.supports: Zurich went to war; the armies met near Kappel (place Kappel am Albis)

sources.title: HLS: Kappelerkriege
sources.quote: Im Ersten Kappelerkrieg von 1529 konnten Kriegshandlungen auf diplomatischem Weg verhindert werden.
sources.supports: They did not fight

sources.title: HLS: Kappelerkriege
sources.quote: Kriegsleute aus beiden Lagern hätten demnach aus einem grossen Eimer an der Grenze gemeinsam eine Suppe aus Milch und Brot gegessen
sources.supports: The story of the milk soup

sources.title: HLS: Kappelerkriege
sources.quote: Dieser fiel am 26. Juni 1529 in Form des Ersten Kappeler Landfriedens eher zugunsten der reformierten Wünsche aus
sources.supports: The First Peace of Kappel (26 June 1529) favoured the Reformed side

sources.title: HLS: Kappelerkriege
sources.quote: Die Frage, ob in den gemeinen Herrschaften die einzelnen Gemeinden oder die regierenden Orte
sources.supports: Layer Mixed: in the common lordships the faith was disputed

stops.title: Kappel: Zwingli is killed
text: In May 1531 Zurich and Bern blocked grain and salt supplies to the Catholic places. In October 1531 the five Catholic places attacked.
On 11 October 1531 they beat the Zurich army at Kappel. About 500 men from Zurich died, among them the reformer Huldrych Zwingli, who went with the army as a preacher.
In the night of 23 to 24 October the Catholics beat Reformed troops again at the Gubel, near Menzingen.

sources.title: HLS: Kappelerkriege
sources.quote: im Mai entschlossen, gegen die fünf Orte eine Proviantsperre (Unterbindung der Zufuhr von Getreide und Salz) zu erlassen
sources.supports: In May 1531 Zurich and Bern blocked grain and salt

sources.title: HLS: Kappelerkriege
sources.quote: Im Oktober 1531 entschlossen sich die fünf inneren Orte, in welchen sich die Lebensmittelblockade immer stärker bemerkbar machte, zum Angriff
sources.supports: In October 1531 the five Catholic places attacked (layer Catholic)

sources.title: HLS: Kappelerkriege
sources.quote: Der um 16 Uhr ausgelöste Angriff der fünf Orte führte nach kurzem Widerstand zur Flucht des in Panik geratenen Zürcher Heeres.
sources.supports: On 11 October 1531 they beat the Zurich army at Kappel (place Kappel am Albis)

sources.title: HLS: Kappelerkriege
sources.quote: Unter den etwa 500 gefallenen Zürchern befand sich auch Zwingli, der das Banner als Feldprediger begleitet hatte
sources.supports: About 500 men from Zurich died, among them Zwingli, who went with the army as a preacher

sources.title: HLS: Kappelerkriege
sources.quote: nur den Gubel bei Menzingen, wo es während des Nachtlagers von einer kleinen Truppe der fünf Orte überfallen und in die Flucht geschlagen wurde
sources.supports: The Catholics beat Reformed troops at the Gubel near Menzingen (place Gubel)

sources.title: HLS: Kappelerkriege
sources.quote: bis zur Nacht vom 23. auf den 24. Okotber 1531
sources.supports: The night of 23 to 24 October 1531

stops.title: Second Peace of Kappel
text: The Second Peace of Kappel (20 November 1531) said that each place keeps its own faith. In the common subject lands, the Catholic side gained.
The Catholic places now had more power in the Confederation. The peace shaped the map of the two faiths for a long time.

sources.title: HLS: Kappelerkriege
sources.quote: jedem einzelnen Ort, die Konfession seiner Bürger und Untertanen selbst zu bestimmen, begünstigte jedoch in den gemeinen Herrschaften den Katholizismus
sources.supports: Each place keeps its own faith; in the common lands the Catholic side gained (layer Mixed)

sources.title: HLS: Kappelerkriege
sources.quote: der am 20. November 1531 im Weiler Deinikon bei Baar abgeschlossene Zweite Kappeler Landfrieden
sources.supports: The Second Peace of Kappel, 20 November 1531 (place Kappel am Albis)

sources.title: HLS: Landfriedensbünde
sources.quote: Die Niederlagen der Reformierten bei Kappel und am Gubel ermöglichten es den fünf Orten, nun einen Frieden nach ihren Bedingungen zu diktieren.
sources.supports: The Catholic places now had more power (place Gubel)

sources.title: HLS: Kappelerkriege
sources.quote: Der Ausgang des Zweiten Kappelerkriegs prägte die konfessionelle Landkarte der Eidgenossenschaft – mit Ausnahme der Westschweiz.
sources.supports: The peace shaped the map of the two faiths

stops.title: The Peasants' War
text: After the Thirty Years' War, prices for farm products fell. In December 1652 Bern, Solothurn and Fribourg also made their coins worth less. The farmers lost money and were angry.

In February 1653 the farmers of the Entlebuch rose against Lucerne. Farmers in the Emmental and in the lands of Solothurn and Basel joined them. In May 1653 they swore an alliance at Huttwil. They wanted their own assemblies and a say in the laws.
This time Catholic and Reformed farmers worked together, against the town lords.

layers.name: Town governments
layers.label: Lands of Lucerne, Bern, Solothurn and Basel (rough)

sources.title: HLS: Bauernkrieg (1653)
sources.quote: Mit der Beendigung des Dreissigjährigen Kriegs folgte auf die ausgeprägte, mehr als zwei Jahrzehnte dauernde Export- und Preiskonjunktur eine tiefe Nachkriegs- und Friedensdepression.
sources.supports: After the Thirty Years' War, prices fell

sources.title: HLS: Bauernkrieg (1653)
sources.quote: Die nach dem Dreissigjährigen Krieg verfügte Abwertung der Berner, Solothurner und Freiburger Handmünzen (Batzen, deshalb auch «Batzenkrieg») im Dezember 1652
sources.supports: Bern, Solothurn and Fribourg made their coins worth less in December 1652

sources.title: HLS: Bauernkrieg (1653)
sources.quote: Die Untertanen der Luzerner Talschaft Entlebuch waren von der Massnahme besonders stark betroffen
sources.supports: The farmers lost money (Entlebuch)

sources.title: HLS: Bauernkrieg (1653)
sources.quote: Am 10. Februar veranstalteten sämtliche Bewohner der Talschaft eine Prozession zur Wallfahrtskirche Heiligkreuz
sources.supports: In February 1653 the Entlebuch rose against Lucerne (place Entlebuch)

sources.title: HLS: Bauernkrieg (1653)
sources.quote: den Aufstand ländlicher Untertanen der eidgenössischen Stände Luzern, Bern, Solothurn und Basel im Entlebuch, Emmental, in Teilen der Solothurner und Basler Landschaft
sources.supports: Farmers in the Emmental, Solothurn and Basel lands joined (layers Rising farmers, Town governments)

sources.title: HLS: Bauernkrieg (1653)
sources.quote: besammelten sich Vertreter der Untertanen von Luzern, Bern, Solothurn und Basel in Huttwil zu einer weiteren Landsgemeinde und schlossen einen dritten «Bauernbund»
sources.supports: In May 1653 (14 May) they swore an alliance at Huttwil (place Huttwil)

sources.title: HLS: Bauernkrieg (1653)
sources.quote: das seit dem Stanser Verkommnis (1481) verweigerte Recht auf eigene politische «Landsgemeinden» und Versammlungen sowie die institutionalisierte Mitsprache an der herrschaftlichen Gesetzgebung
sources.supports: They wanted their own assemblies and a say in the laws

sources.title: HLS: Bauernkrieg (1653)
sources.quote: intensive Markt- und Austauschbeziehungen, welche über die territorialherrschaftlichen und konfessionellen Grenzen hinwegschritten
sources.supports: Catholic and Reformed farmers worked together across borders

stops.title: Wohlenschwil and Herzogenbuchsee
text: The Diet (the meeting of the Confederate places) sent an army. On 3 June 1653 it fought the farmers at Wohlenschwil, and the church and part of the village burned. Then Bernese troops under General Sigmund von Erlach beat the rest of the farmers' army at Herzogenbuchsee, and that village burned too.
The farmers' leader, Niklaus Leuenberger, was betrayed and executed in Bern with 20 other leaders. The town lords won, but after this they could not make their power absolute.

layers.name: Town governments
layers.label: Lands of Lucerne, Bern, Solothurn and Basel (rough)

sources.title: HLS: Wohlenschwil
sources.quote: am 3.6.1653 zwischen dem Tagsatzungsheer und den aufständ. Bauern bei W. zum Gefecht. Die Kirche und ein Teil des Dorfs gingen dabei in Flammen auf.
sources.supports: On 3 June 1653 the Diet army fought the farmers at Wohlenschwil; the church and part of the village burned (place Wohlenschwil)

sources.title: HLS: Leuenberger, Niklaus
sources.quote: nach dem Zusammenbruch der Aufstandsbewegung infolge der Niederlagen der Bauern bei Wohlenschwil und Herzogenbuchsee
sources.supports: The farmers were beaten at Wohlenschwil and Herzogenbuchsee

sources.title: HLS: Herzogenbuchsee
sources.quote: Bei Herzogenbuchsee besiegten dann bernische Truppen unter General Sigmund von Erlach Reste von Niklaus Leuenbergers Bauernheer
sources.supports: Bernese troops under Sigmund von Erlach beat the rest of the farmers' army at Herzogenbuchsee (place Herzogenbuchsee)

sources.title: HLS: Herzogenbuchsee
sources.quote: das Dorf ging in Flammen auf
sources.supports: The village of Herzogenbuchsee burned

sources.title: HLS: Leuenberger, Niklaus
sources.quote: von einem ehem. Mitstreiter verraten, nach Bern abgeführt und mit 20 weiteren Anführern hingerichtet
sources.supports: Leuenberger was betrayed and executed in Bern with 20 other leaders

sources.title: HLS: Leuenberger, Niklaus
sources.quote: Nachdem er auch die beiden folgenden Landsgemeinden von Huttwil geleitet hatte
sources.supports: Place Huttwil: farmers' alliance

sources.title: HLS: Bauernkrieg (1653)
sources.quote: dass die städtischen Obrigkeiten in der Alten Eidgenossenschaft die Entwicklung zum Absolutismus nicht weitertreiben konnten
sources.supports: After this the town lords could not make their power absolute (layer Town governments)

stops.title: First Villmergen War
text: In 1655 Reformed people from Arth fled to Zurich, and Schwyz executed four Reformed people who had stayed. Zurich and Bern wanted to change the Peace of Kappel by force.
Zurich laid siege to Rapperswil but could not take it. On 24 January 1656 troops from Lucerne and Zug beat the Bernese army at Villmergen.
The Third Peace of Baden (March 1656) kept the old rules. The Catholic places kept their stronger position.

layers.name: Catholic
layers.label: Catholic side: the five inner places

sources.title: HLS: Villmergerkrieg, Erster
sources.quote: Im September 1655 traf eine Gruppe von reformierten Flüchtlingen (Nikodemiten) aus Arth in Zürich ein.
sources.supports: In 1655 Reformed people from Arth fled to Zurich

sources.title: HLS: Villmergerkrieg, Erster
sources.quote: Entgegen Berner Warnungen wurden vier in Schwyz verbliebene Reformierte hingerichtet.
sources.supports: Schwyz executed four Reformed people

sources.title: HLS: Villmergerkrieg, Erster
sources.quote: Die beiden reformierten Orte schickten sich damit an, die Rechtsordnung des Zweiten Landfriedens von 1531 umzugestalten und kriegerische Wege zu beschreiten.
sources.supports: Zurich and Bern wanted to change the Peace of Kappel by force

sources.title: HLS: Villmergerkrieg, Erster
sources.quote: Militärischer Konflikt zwischen den reformierten Orten Zürich, Bern und Schaffhausen und den fünf katholischen Orten
sources.supports: Layers: Reformed side Zurich, Bern, Schaffhausen; Catholic side the five inner places

sources.title: HLS: Villmergerkrieg, Erster
sources.quote: Als sein Sturmangriff auf Rapperswil am 3. Februar misslang
sources.supports: Zurich could not take Rapperswil (place Rapperswil)

sources.title: HLS: Villmergerkrieg, Erster
sources.quote: In einem Überraschungsangriff schlugen Luzerner und Zuger Truppen unter Christoph Pfyffer das Berner Heer bei Villmergen.
sources.supports: Troops from Lucerne and Zug beat the Bernese army at Villmergen (place Villmergen)

sources.title: HLS: Villmergerkrieg, Erster
sources.quote: Die Entscheidung zugunsten der katholischen Orte – Freiburg und Solothurn waren neutral geblieben – fiel am 24. Januar 1656.
sources.supports: On 24 January 1656; other places were neutral (layer Others)

sources.title: HLS: Villmergerkrieg, Erster
sources.quote: endete mit dem Abschluss des Dritten Landfriedens zu Baden am 7. März 1656
sources.supports: The Third Peace of Baden, March 1656

sources.title: HLS: Villmergerkrieg, Erster
sources.quote: eine Erneuerung des Status quo ante, indem der Zweite Landfrieden von 1531 bestätigt wurde
sources.supports: The peace kept the old rules

sources.title: HLS: Villmergerkrieg, Erster
sources.quote: Die Stellung der inneren Orte, die eine Kompetenzvermehrung eidgenössischer Institutionen vor allem in konfessionellen Streitigkeiten ablehnten, wurde gestärkt.
sources.supports: The Catholic places kept their stronger position

stops.title: Second Villmergen War
text: The war started in the Toggenburg, where people rose against their lord, the abbot of St. Gallen. Zurich and Bern supported them. The five Catholic places took the abbot's side.
On 25 July 1712 Bern beat the Catholic army at Villmergen. In the Peace of Aarau (11 August 1712) the Catholics lost their share in ruling the county of Baden and the lower Freie Ämter.
Now Zurich and Bern were the strongest powers in the Confederation. Both faiths had equal rights in the common lands.

layers.name: Baden and lower Freie Ämter
layers.label: Baden and lower Freie Ämter: now ruled by Zurich, Bern and Glarus (rough)

layers.name: Catholic
layers.label: Catholic side: the five inner places

sources.title: HLS: Villmergerkrieg, Zweiter
sources.quote: der als überkonfessioneller Untertanenaufstand der Toggenburger gegen ihren Landesherrn begann
sources.supports: The war started in the Toggenburg with a rising against the abbot (layer Toggenburg)

sources.title: HLS: Villmergerkrieg, Zweiter
sources.quote: Zürich und Bern unterstützten dieses Vorgehen und richteten am 13. April 1712 ein Manifest gegen den Fürstabt
sources.supports: Zurich and Bern supported them; the five Catholic places took the abbot's side (layers Reformed, Catholic)

sources.title: HLS: Villmergerkrieg, Zweiter
sources.quote: worauf die fünf inneren Orte auf die Seite des Fürstabts traten
sources.supports: The five Catholic places took the abbot's side

sources.title: HLS: Villmergerkrieg, Zweiter
sources.quote: Am 25. Juli kam es zum entscheidenden Treffen der Innerschweizer und Berner Truppen bei Villmergen
sources.supports: On 25 July 1712 Bern beat the Catholic army at Villmergen (place Villmergen)

sources.title: HLS: Villmergerkrieg, Zweiter
sources.quote: der mit dem Sieg der besser ausgerüsteten und ausgebildeten Berner endete
sources.supports: Bern won

sources.title: HLS: Villmergerkrieg, Zweiter
sources.quote: dem am 11. August 1712 in Aarau abgeschlossenen Vierten Landfrieden
sources.supports: The Peace of Aarau, 11 August 1712 (place Aarau)

sources.title: HLS: Landfriedensbünde
sources.quote: Die fünf Orte wurden von der Mitherrschaft in der Grafschaft Baden (mit Bremgarten) und in den Unteren Freien Ämtern ausgeschlossen
sources.supports: The Catholics lost their share in Baden and the lower Freie Ämter (layer Baden and lower Freie Ämter)

sources.title: HLS: Villmergerkrieg, Zweiter
sources.quote: Der Vierte Landfrieden war ein Machtfrieden der Berner und Zürcher.
sources.supports: Zurich and Bern were now the strongest powers

sources.title: HLS: Villmergerkrieg, Zweiter
sources.quote: Der Friedensschluss legte die Rechtsgleichheit der beiden Konfessionen in Religionsfragen fest
sources.supports: Both faiths had equal rights

uncertain: After 1712 Glarus shared with Zurich and Bern in ruling Baden and the lower Freie Ämter (map label).

notes: Religion areas are today's cantons and are rough: Glarus, Appenzell, Thurgau, St. Gallen, Graubünden and Aargau were mixed or split; the town of St. Gallen was Reformed. Areas of the 1653 rising are today's districts, rough. The Huttwil oath date differs (4 or 14 May 1653, old and new calendar). The 'milk soup' of 1529 is a traditional story. The exact day of Herzogenbuchsee (June 1653) was not checked in HLS, so the text says 'a few days later'.

title: 1798-1799: foreign armies in Switzerland
card: France ended the old Confederation, and in 1799 French, Austrian and Russian armies fought on Swiss soil.

stops.title: French troops in Vaud
text: After the revolution of 1789, France became a strong and aggressive power. At the end of 1797 it took the south of the Bishopric of Basel. Many people in the subject lands, such as Vaud, were unhappy with their rulers.

In January 1798 a revolution broke out in Vaud, and on 24 January the 'Lemanic Republic' was declared. French troops marched in. Other places also freed their subjects. The old order of the Confederation broke down.

layers.name: France
layers.label: France, with the former Bishopric of Basel (rough)

layers.name: Vaud
layers.label: Vaud, now free of Bern, with French troops

sources.title: HLS: Franzoseneinfall
sources.quote: Frankreich , das im Laufe der 1790er Jahre immer mehr in eine durch die Französische Revolution ausgelöste Dynamik geriet
sources.supports: France changed after the revolution (layer France)

sources.title: HLS: Franzoseneinfall
sources.quote: Ende 1797 besetzten französische Truppen den südlichen, in die eidgenössische Neutralität eingeschlossenen Teil des Fürstbistums Basel.
sources.supports: At the end of 1797 France took the south of the Bishopric of Basel

sources.title: HLS: Helvetische Republik
sources.quote: Frankreich nutzte die bestehende Unzufriedenheit der ländlichen Eliten in den Untertanengebieten
sources.supports: Many people in the subject lands were unhappy

sources.title: HLS: Franzoseneinfall
sources.quote: Nach dem Ausbruch der Helvetischen Revolution in der Waadt und aufgrund eines Hilfegesuches der am 24. Januar 1798 proklamierten Lemanischen Republik marschierten die Franzosen ein.
sources.supports: Revolution in Vaud; Lemanic Republic on 24 January 1798; French troops marched in (layer Vaud; place Lausanne)

sources.title: HLS: Helvetische Republik
sources.quote: griff die Helvetische Revolution rasch auf andere Orte über
sources.supports: Other places followed

sources.title: HLS: Helvetische Republik
sources.quote: April 1798 gab es in der Schweiz kein einziges Untertanengebiet mehr
sources.supports: The subjects were freed; the old order broke down (layer Confederates)

stops.title: Grauholz and Neuenegg: Bern falls
text: Bern decided to fight. French armies attacked from the south-west (Vaud) and from the north (the former Bishopric of Basel).

On 4 March 1798 the Bernese government resigned. Its troops still fought: in early March the French beat them at Fraubrunnen and then at the Grauholz, north of Bern. In the south, Bernese troops stopped the French at Neuenegg. But this came too late.
Bern gave up, and French troops occupied the town. They took the Bernese state treasure.

layers.name: France
layers.label: France, with the former Bishopric of Basel (rough)

sources.title: HLS: Franzoseneinfall
sources.quote: Das aristokratische Bern und die mit ihm verbündeten Patriziate von Solothurn und Freiburg sahen sich dadurch von Norden und Süden bedroht.
sources.supports: French armies attacked from the north and the south (layer France)

sources.title: HLS: Helvetische Republik
sources.quote: in einer Zangenbewegung von der Waadt und vom Jura her in das westliche Mittelland vorstiessen
sources.supports: From Vaud and from the Jura (layer French-held)

sources.title: HLS: Franzoseneinfall
sources.quote: Am 4. März 1798 dankte die Berner Regierung ab.
sources.supports: On 4 March 1798 the Bernese government resigned

stops.title: The Helvetic Republic
text: On 12 April 1798 the Helvetic Republic replaced the old Confederation. Its first capital was Aarau. It was one state with one constitution, made after the French model. All people now had the same rights; there were no more subject lands.

Schwyz, Uri and Nidwalden refused the new constitution. Their troops, led by Alois Reding of Schwyz, won some fights, for example at Rothenthurm. But the French army was too strong, and on 4 May 1798 Schwyz gave up.

stops.title: Nidwalden: the days of terror
text: In July 1798 every citizen had to swear an oath to the new state. Nidwalden refused and rose up. The Helvetic government asked the French army under General Schauenburg to put down the rising.

On 9 September 1798 the people of Nidwalden fought a hopeless battle against the French army. HLS gives about 100 dead fighters from Nidwalden and about as many French. More than 300 men, women and children were killed afterwards. Stans, Stansstad, Buochs and Ennetmoos were badly destroyed.
People in Nidwalden remembered these days of terror for a long time.

stops.title: First Battle of Zurich
text: In 1799 Austria and Russia went to war against France again (the Second Coalition War). Switzerland became a battlefield of foreign armies.

Austrian troops came from the north under Archduke Charles and from the east under Friedrich von Hotze. In early June 1799 they attacked the French under General Masséna at Zurich. The French gave up the town and moved back to a line west of Zurich.
The armies took food, animals and wood from the people. Many villages suffered badly.

text: In late August most Austrian troops left. A Russian army of about 20,000 men under General Korsakov took their place at Zurich.
On 25 and 26 September 1799 Masséna attacked and beat the Russians at Zurich. On the same days French troops beat the Austrians at the Linth river near Schänis.
The plan of the allies was to attack the French together with a second Russian army coming from Italy. That army, under General Suvorov, was still in the mountains.

stops.title: Suvorov crosses the Gotthard
text: The Russian general Alexander Suvorov had driven the French out of northern Italy. Now he was to join Korsakov at Zurich. His army had about 20,000 men.

After fights at Faido and Airolo he reached the Gotthard pass on 24 September 1799. Then his troops fought hard against the French in the Schöllenen gorge, at the Devil's Bridge. On 26 September he reached Altdorf.
There was no road along Lake Lucerne, and the French held the boats. So Suvorov had to go over the mountains.

stops.title: Over the Panix pass
text: The way north was blocked, because the Austrians had also lost at Schänis. Suvorov turned south. On 6 and 7 October 1799 his army crossed the Panix pass, about 2,400 metres high, in deep snow. Snow and cold cost him many men and much material.
The army reached the Vorderrhein valley at Ilanz. On 12 October it left Graubünden over the St. Luzisteig and marched back to Russia. The march did not change the war.
For the local people, the march brought hunger and loss. French troops stayed in Switzerland. In 1803 Napoleon gave the country a new order, the Act of Mediation.

title: The Sonderbund War and the federal state
card: In November 1847 the last civil war lasted less than a month, and in 1848 modern Switzerland was born.

stops.title: The Sonderbund
text: In the 1840s liberals and Catholic conservatives fought over the future of Switzerland. The liberals wanted a federal state. The conservatives wanted the cantons to stay free, and they defended the Catholic religion.
Lucerne decided to call the Jesuits, and they came to Lucerne in 1845. Armed groups of radicals (the 'Freischaren') attacked Lucerne twice, in 1844 and 1845, but failed.

On 11 December 1845 seven Catholic conservative cantons formed a defence league in Lucerne: Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden (Obwalden and Nidwalden), Zug, Fribourg and Valais. Its opponents called it the 'Sonderbund' (separate league).

stops.title: The Diet decides
text: The federal treaty did not allow such separate leagues. In May 1847 the liberals won the elections in St. Gallen, and so they had a majority in the Diet, the meeting of the cantons.

text: One after the other, the other Sonderbund cantons gave up: Zug on 21 November, then the inner cantons and Valais between 25 and 29 November.

stops.title: The federal state
text: The winners wrote a new constitution. On 12 September 1848 it came into force. Switzerland was now a federal state with a government (the Federal Council) and a parliament with two equal chambers. Customs inside Switzerland were abolished, and money became a federal matter.

On 28 November 1848 parliament chose Bern as the federal city. The cantons kept many rights. The Catholic conservatives were the losers for a long time; they got a seat in the Federal Council only in 1891.
The Sonderbund War was the last war between Swiss cantons.
